summary: This unit teaches you to plan, deliver and evaluate a community education project: finding out what a community needs, setting SMART aims and learning outcomes, designing sessions that suit adult learners, working with partners, budgeting, promoting the project, keeping everyone safe, facilitating sessions, and measuring and reporting results. It is written for supervisors and managers in community, health, social and public-sector work in Jamaica.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It prepares you to run **community education projects**: short, planned programmes that help residents learn something useful and change what they do. Examples are dengue prevention, hurricane preparedness, family budgeting, safe disposal of waste, road safety and healthy eating.

The people who run these projects work in municipal corporations, health departments, schools, churches, citizens' associations, youth clubs, non-governmental organisations and agencies of the Government of Jamaica. At Level 5 you are the **project coordinator**: you do not only teach, you plan the whole project, manage the money, partners and volunteers, and answer to the funder and the community.

**Who it is for:** supervisors, officers and managers who are asked to lead or support education work in a community, and trainees who want to show they can manage a project from first idea to final report.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Find out what the community needs
Use surveys, focus groups and existing records to learn what residents already know, do and need, and take a baseline.
Set aims, objectives and learning outcomes
Write a clear aim, SMART objectives and learning outcomes that say what participants will be able to do.
Choose methods and materials that suit adult learners, reading levels, culture, age and access needs.
Agree roles with partners in writing, and present a costed proposal to a funder.
Plan and manage the budget and schedule
Cost each line, add it up twice, and keep to the timetable and the grant.
Promote the project and manage risk
Reach the target group through the right channels, and plan for weather, low turnout, safeguarding and other risks.
Run sessions that involve everyone, handle difficult moments, protect confidentiality and keep people safe.
Evaluate, report and make results last
Measure results against the baseline, report honestly to the funder and build in ways to keep the benefits going.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenario questions on needs, planning, delivery, budgeting, safeguarding and evaluation, including short sums.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as needs assessment, baseline, peer educator) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks** done in a group: a project plan pack built from a needs pack, and a 30-minute session delivered, quizzed and evaluated. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: In every sum, work it twice, by two different routes. Examiners and funders both notice a budget that does not add up.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Understanding the community: the needs assessment

blocks.p: A community education project starts with the **community**, not with your idea. A **needs assessment** is the process of finding out what a community already knows, does and needs before you plan anything. Without it you may teach people what they already know, use methods that do not suit them, or solve a problem they do not have.

ul: **Who** lives there: numbers, ages, jobs, reading levels, languages used day to day, disabilities.
**What they know and do now**: for example, do households cover water drums? Do they have a family hurricane plan?
**What stops them** changing: cost, time, distance, habit, belief, lack of services.
**What already exists**: clinics, schools, churches, clubs, earlier projects, and why they did or did not work.

head: Method
What it gives you
Watch out for
rows: Existing data (clinic or health office records, municipal corporation complaints, school and police figures, census data)
Facts that cost little and cover the whole area
May be old or incomplete; may not say why people act as they do
Household survey (short questionnaire, by interview where reading levels are low)
Numbers you can count and compare, and later repeat
Sample must cover all streets and groups, not only people who are easy to reach
Focus group (a small, guided group discussion, about 6 to 10 people)
The reasons behind the numbers; views on what would work
Hold separate groups where some people may not speak freely, such as young men, women or the elderly
Interviews with leaders and service providers
Local knowledge, history and offers of help
Leaders speak for some people, not for everyone
Observation and walk-through (for example, a yard check or a look at dumping sites)
What people actually do, not only what they say
Get permission; do not judge or embarrass anyone

blocks.p: The fullest picture comes from **using several methods together** (sometimes called triangulation): records show the size of the problem, a survey counts it, and focus groups explain it.

Residents should help plan the project, not only attend it. When people are involved from the start, the project fits real needs and they feel **ownership**, so they promote it, turn up and keep going after it ends. Work through the citizens' association, community development committees, churches, schools, and respected local people. In Jamaica, the Social Development Commission (SDC) and the municipal corporation's community officers often know the groups and leaders in an area.

If two groups want the project to focus on different issues, do not pick the louder leader and do not drop the project. Show both groups the evidence, agree priorities openly, and explain the choice. A simple **scoring grid** can help: score each possible topic for need, community support, cost and whether you can deliver it, then add the scores (weight the most important criterion higher if the group agrees).

A **baseline** is the starting measurement, taken before the project begins, that later results are compared with. Examples: the percentage of yards with mosquito breeding sites; the average score on a short quiz; the number of households with a written family plan; helmet-wearing counts at three junctions. You cannot show a change unless you know where you started. Plan the baseline at the planning stage, and use the **same method, places and times** when you measure again.

blocks.note: Learning needs are not the same as wants. Residents may ask for a concert; the evidence may show that the real need is safe water storage. Listen to both, and let the evidence and the residents' priorities together shape the project.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Before a project on a sensitive topic such as family budgets or abuse, explain how information will be used, ask only what you need and keep answers confidential. Never ask people to give details of their debts, health or family problems in front of others.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Plan from the top down: the **aim** says what the project is for; **objectives** say what the project will achieve and by when; **learning outcomes** say what a participant will be able to do after a session. Each level supports the one above it.

head: Level
What it states
Example: hurricane preparedness in a coastal district
rows: The overall purpose, in one sentence
To help families in the district prepare for the hurricane season
A specific result for the whole project, written to the SMART test
By 31 May, 150 households will have a written family plan with a meeting point and an emergency contact list
What a participant can do at the end of a session
At the end of the session, participants can pack a basic emergency kit from a checklist

head: Letter
Test
Weak objective
Better objective
rows: Specific: says exactly what will change and for whom
Increase the number of adults in the district who check blood pressure at the clinic
Achievable: possible with your time, money and people
Reach every household in the parish in a month
Visit 300 households in three months with 12 trained volunteers
Relevant: linked to the need you found
Teach residents to remove breeding sites, as the survey showed was the gap

blocks.p: Start with the words 'participants can ...' and use an **action verb you can observe**: compare, list, demonstrate, calculate, complete, explain, choose. Avoid verbs you cannot observe, such as 'understand', 'know about' or 'appreciate'. 'Participants can compare the sugar in two drink labels' is a good outcome because you can watch it being done; 'participants will understand nutrition' is not.

An **output** is what the project produces or does (sessions held, leaflets printed, people trained). An **outcome** is the change that results (more households with a plan, fewer breeding sites). Funders want both, but they care most about outcomes. Counting leaflets handed out does not show that anyone learned anything.

blocks.note: A good test of an objective: could a stranger, a year later, check from the records whether it was met? If not, it is not yet specific, measurable or time-bound.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Adults want to know **why** they are learning something and how it solves their own problems.
They bring **experience**. Ask for it and use it; do not talk down to people.
They learn best by **doing**: demonstrations, practice, discussion and problem-solving, not long lectures.
They need respect, choice and a comfortable setting. Fear of looking foolish stops many adults taking part, especially where reading is weak.

head: Method
Best for
Limits
rows: Reaches only those who can attend at that time
Changing practical behaviour, for example storing chemicals safely, covering a water drum
Reaching the elderly, people with low literacy, and tailoring advice to each home
Needs many trained volunteers and much time
Reaching many people quickly and repeating key messages
One-way; cannot check understanding; data and signal may be limited in rural areas
Trusted messages from people like the audience, for example young riders teaching riders

blocks.p: A **mix** of methods usually works best. A single radio advert or poster seldom changes what people do. A demonstration followed by practice, backed by a reminder, often does.

ul: Use **plain words, short sentences and pictures**, especially where reading levels are low. Spoken explanation and demonstration matter more than handouts.
Use **local examples**, local foods, local voices and places that residents recognise.
Keep content **accurate**: take medical, safety and legal information only from the proper authorities such as the health authorities. Never include a home remedy or rumour, however well meant.
**Pilot-test** drafts with a few people from the target group before printing a large number. Print only when they understand it.
Make print large enough to read, with good contrast.

blocks.p: Respect local customs, beliefs and the busy times in the community (reaping season, market days, church days, school terms). Include respected local people, but remember that **using local voices does not remove your duty to give accurate information**.

head: Group
Barrier
Response
rows: Steps, long sitting, poor sight or hearing, transport
Step-free venue, seats with backs, shade, toilets, short sessions with breaks, large print, clear speech
Ask at registration what support is needed; ramp, interpreter, helper, alternative formats
Pictures, demonstration, spoken explanation, show of hands or picture cards
Evening or weekend options, a children's corner, a daytime session
Young men or other hard-to-reach groups
Do not see the project as for them
Ask them when, where and how they would join; use peer educators and their own channels

flow: Choose methods and activities that let participants practise
Prepare accurate materials and a timed outline
Check the venue, equipment and a back-up plan
Plan how you will check learning (a before-and-after quiz, show of hands, practice task)

blocks.note: Always have a back-up. If the projector fails, a printed copy and a flipchart let the session go on. If a storm warning is issued, have a postponement plan and a way to tell participants.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Partners bring what you lack: accurate information, a trusted voice, a venue, volunteers, equipment, money. Choose partners for their **value to this project**: for a water and sanitation project, the local public health office; for a hurricane project, the national disaster agency, the municipal corporation and local response teams; for a financial literacy project, a credit union.

head: Possible partner
What it may offer
What it may want
rows: Reaching its own targets; being named correctly
Trusted voice, hall, volunteers, access to families
Respect for its values; use of facilities cared for
A real say in the project
Permission, venue, community officers, waste collection

blocks.p: Confirm each arrangement in a **short written agreement** (a letter of agreement or memorandum) setting out roles, contributions, dates, costs, use of logos, how money is handled and who speaks to the media. A spoken promise after church is not enough. A small steering group with one person from each partner keeps everyone informed.

blocks.note: Keep the project open to all. If a political candidate or party offers money on condition that its colours or name appear on project materials, decline. Accepting would turn a community project into a party event and put off residents.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A funder wants to see a **clear need** (the evidence), **objectives and outcomes**, a **costed budget**, how you will **measure and report** results, who will do the work, and how benefits will **last**. Do not promise what you cannot deliver; a promise that every child will read perfectly is not credible.

List every cost line: venue, materials and printing, facilitators, refreshments, transport, promotion, equipment, evaluation, insurance and other costs, and a small **contingency**. Show the working: unit cost times quantity times number of sessions. Add the lines in two different orders to check.

ul: **Cost per participant** = total cost divided by the number of participants. If 60 people complete the project: J$210,000 / 60 = J$3,500 each.
**Overspend as a percentage** = (actual minus budget) / budget x 100. Printing budgeted at J$40,000 but costing J$46,000 is J$6,000 over, which is 15% over budget.
**Reach** = number reached / number in the target population x 100. 1,200 of 1,600 households is 75%.

blocks.p: Keep **receipts and records** for all spending, and report spending against the budget. Never pay people in cash without a signed record. Funders and auditors will ask for them.

Draw a timetable (a simple table or Gantt chart) that runs from needs assessment to the final report, with a named person for each task. Count carefully: six weekly sessions starting on Saturday 4 April end on Saturday 9 May (the sixth session is five weeks after the first). Build in time for printing, approvals and a possible postponement.

blocks.note: A funder's cost per participant and your own cost per participant should use the same count. Say whether you mean those who registered or those who completed the course.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Even a good project fails if residents do not know about it. Match the channel to the audience. If a quick check shows most people did not hear about the sessions, do not blame residents and do not cancel: promote through the places and people they trust.

head: Audience
Useful channels
rows: Church announcements, community health aides, word of mouth, radio, notices at shops and clinics
Schools, parent-teacher meetings, children's take-home notes
Social media, WhatsApp groups, sports clubs, bike stands
Market notices, trade associations, short messages at quiet times

ul: Give **date, time, place, who it is for, what it costs (free), and a contact number**.
Repeat the message more than once.
Ask each partner to carry it to their own members.

blocks.p: A **risk** is something that might go wrong and affect the project. For each risk, state the likelihood, the effect, who is responsible and what you will do about it. Keep this in a simple risk register.

head: Risk
Likelihood and effect
Action
rows: Storm warning, flooding or heavy rain, especially in the hurricane season
Flexible dates, postponement plan, indoor venue on higher ground, a way to tell people quickly
Early promotion, reminders by WhatsApp, a convenient time, find out why people stay away
Monthly budget check, contingency, approval for changes
Back-up printed material, spare batteries, a flipchart
Low but severe; harm to people
Vetting, code of conduct, trained staff, first aid, referral procedure
Reserve list, clear roles, support and thanks

blocks.p: **Safeguarding** means protecting children and vulnerable adults from harm. If volunteers will work with children (for example aged 10 to 14), the coordinator must make sure that:

ul: Every volunteer is **vetted** before starting: an application form, references, and a police record check, in line with the organisation's safeguarding policy. This is not the same as being related to a child, and it has nothing to do with a degree.
Volunteers are **trained** in the code of conduct and what to do if a child discloses abuse.
No volunteer is ever **alone with a child** out of sight of others; activities happen in open view, with at least two adults present.
Contact with children is through the project and parents, not private messages.

There is a named **safeguarding lead** and a clear **referral procedure** to the proper child protection authorities. Suspected child abuse must be reported; the law and the organisation's policy require it.

blocks.h: When someone tells you something serious

flow: Listen calmly and take it seriously
Do not promise to keep it secret; explain you may need to tell someone who can help
Do not investigate, question closely or confront anyone
Record what was said, in the person's own words, as soon as possible
Tell the named safeguarding lead and follow the referral procedure
Protect confidentiality: share only with those who need to know

ul: If a participant shares private details (such as debts) in a session, **keep them confidential**, never use the story by name, and remind everyone of the ground rules: what is said here stays here.

Get **informed consent** (free agreement after being told what it involves) before taking or using photographs, and consent from a parent or guardian for any child. An open event does not mean consent for publication.
Store registers, forms and photographs securely and use them only for the stated purpose. Follow the data protection law and your organisation's rules.
Use only information from the proper authorities. A home remedy a volunteer has heard about is not a project message.

Follow safety rules in demonstrations. When showing how to make a mild bleach solution for cleaning water containers, follow the label, wear gloves, work in a ventilated place, **never mix** it with other cleaners and keep children away from the chemical.
Stay neutral: the project is for all residents, whatever their politics, church or area.

blocks.note: Never promise secrecy. Say instead: 'I will keep this private unless someone is in danger, and then I will tell only the person who can help.'
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Welcome people, introduce the team and agree ground rules (respect, listening, confidentiality, phones on silent)
State the learning outcomes in plain words
Take a short baseline or starter activity (quick quiz, show of hands, question)
Teach in short parts: explain, demonstrate, let people practise
Check understanding with questions and activities
Summarise, agree one action each participant will take, and thank people

ul: **Ask, do not tell**: open questions such as 'What do you do at home when a storm warning is announced?'
**Invite everyone**: if one participant keeps talking over others, thank him, then invite others to share. Do not ignore it and do not remove him.
**Use pairs and small groups** so quiet people can speak.
**Handle disagreement calmly**: restate each view, return to the evidence, and keep to the ground rules.
**Admit what you do not know** and promise to find out from the proper source.
**Watch time** and keep to the plan.

head: Problem
Good response
rows: Thank them, then ask others; give tasks to small groups
Switch to printed copy and flipchart
Start with those present, record the number and find out why; follow up with the people who missed it
Keep it confidential; remind everyone of the ground rules; do not use the story by name
Listen, do not promise secrecy, follow the referral procedure
Provide a children's corner with a responsible adult; do not leave children unsupervised

ul: Recruit with a short **role description**: tasks, hours, behaviour expected.
**Brief and train** before the project; match roles to skills.
Make roles and times clear; if volunteers arrive late or leave early, **talk with them** about the roles, times and support they need before deciding anything.
Say thank you, give feedback and keep a record of hours. Reimburse agreed travel costs.
A **debrief** after each session lets the team note what worked and adjust the next one. It is not for blaming people.

head: Role
Main duties
rows: Keeps the project to plan, budget and timeline; leads partners; reports to the funder
Carries out agreed tasks within the code of conduct
Provides money; receives reports; does not run the project

blocks.note: A debrief takes ten minutes. Ask three questions: What worked? What did not? What will we change next time?
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Monitoring** is checking progress while the project runs (attendance, spending, timetable, risks). **Evaluation** is judging at the end whether the project achieved its aims and what was learned. Plan evaluation **at the planning stage**, with a baseline, not after the last session.

head: Level of evidence
Example
Strength
rows: Shows who took part; does not show learning
Smiley-face cards, show of hands, short feedback
Shows enjoyment and problems; weak evidence of change
Quiz before and after; practice task
Fewer breeding sites in later yard checks; more households with a written plan
Best evidence that what people do has changed
Fewer cases of illness or injury
Strongest, but many things affect it, so use with care

blocks.p: Choose methods that suit participants. People who are not confident writers can give feedback with smiley-face cards, a show of hands, drawings or an interview. A four-page questionnaire or an essay does not suit them.

ul: **Attendance rate:** 120 registered; 96 attended at least five of six sessions. 96 / 120 x 100 = 80%.
**Percentage points:** the quiz average rose from 45% to 72%. 72 - 45 = **27 percentage points**. A rise from 50% to 80% is 30 percentage points. Do not call it '27%' or '60%'.
**Completion rate:** 68 of 80 completed. 68 / 80 x 100 = 85%.
**Cost per participant:** J$270,000 / 180 people = J$1,500.

blocks.note: Percentage and percentage points are different. A score going from 40% to 60% rose by 20 percentage points, which is a 50% increase. Say which you mean.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: If an evaluation shows that a group (for example men aged 20 to 35) hardly attended, do not repeat the same plan and do not decide they are not interested. **Ask them** when, where and how they would take part, and change the design. Report results honestly, including targets missed. A report that hides a missed target damages trust.

The final report should show **results against the aims and objectives**, **spending against the budget** (with explanations of differences), **who was reached**, **lessons learned** and **how benefits will continue**. Add a few photographs only with consent; photographs alone are not a report. Do not list participants' names and phone numbers, and do not use the report to complain about the funder.
**Sustainability** is the project's ability to keep its benefits going after the funding and the project team have gone. Ways to build it:

ul: Train **peer educators**: community members who go on teaching others in their own group.
Hand the work to a **lasting local body** such as a citizens' association, church, school club or CBO, with the materials and a simple plan.
Build the message into **existing services**, such as clinic sessions or the school curriculum.
Leave materials, a WhatsApp group and contacts with the community.

blocks.p: Taking all the materials away, one big final event or free T-shirts do not make results last.

blocks.note: Peer educators need support and recognition (training, certificates, a contact person). Without them, people drift away.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: explain what a needs assessment is and name three ways of carrying one out.
use several methods together and consult residents so the project fits their needs.
take a baseline and say why the same method must be used again at the end.
write an aim, SMART objectives and learning outcomes with observable verbs.
apply the principles of adult learning when choosing methods and designing materials.
adapt sessions for elderly people, people with low literacy, people with disabilities and working parents.
choose partners for value and confirm each arrangement in writing.
prepare a costed budget, add it twice, and work out cost per participant, percentage overspend and reach.
promote a project through the channels the target group uses.
write a risk register and plan for storms, low attendance and overspend.
apply safeguarding rules: vetting, no one alone with a child, a named lead and referral.
keep information confidential, get consent for images, and use only accurate information.
facilitate a session, handle difficult moments and manage volunteers.
measure results with percentages and percentage points, report honestly, and plan for sustainability.

terms: Needs assessment
Finding out what a community knows, does and needs before planning a project.
Baseline
The starting measurement taken before the project, which later results are compared with.
Aim
The overall purpose of the project.
SMART objective
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Learning outcome
What a participant will be able to do by the end of a session.
Output
What the project produces or does, such as sessions held.
Outcome
The change that results, such as more households with a plan.
Focus group
A small, guided group discussion used to explore residents' views.
Peer educator
A trained community member who goes on teaching others in their own group.
Community-based organisation (CBO)
A non-profit group run by and for local residents, such as a citizens' association or youth club.
Contingency
A small amount added to a budget for likely but uncertain extra costs.
Safeguarding
Protecting children and vulnerable adults from harm.
Vetting
Checks on volunteers who will work with children, such as references and a police record check.
Informed consent
A person's free agreement, after being told what it involves, to take part or to be photographed.
Sustainability
The ability to keep a project's benefits going after funding and the project team have gone.
Percentage points
The difference between two percentages, for example 45% to 72% is 27 points.

c1.title: Mosquito-breeding project in Annotto Bay
c1.text: Dian Williams, a community officer, is planning a six-week project in an Annotto Bay district to reduce mosquito breeding in homes. The parish health department's records show a high number of dengue cases. Before the project, a yard check of 120 homes found breeding sites in 54 of them. Her objective is to bring this below 20% of homes (fewer than 24 of the same 120) by 31 December. After the project, a repeat check of the same 120 homes using the same method found breeding sites in 30.

c2.title: Diabetes-diet sessions for elders in Lionel Town
c2.text: A health educator is planning four sessions on healthy eating for adults over 55 in Lionel Town. Many of the elders have limited reading skill, few have smartphones, and the only bus into town runs on market days. Most have lived with diabetes or high blood pressure for years and have strong ideas about food.

c3.title: Black River youth-skills grant
c3.text: A community group in Black River has a grant of J$400,000 for a five-session youth skills programme for 50 participants. Planned costs: printing J$84,000; hall hire J$12,000 per session; facilitator fee J$20,000 per session; refreshments at J$250 per person per session; transport J$48,000. The group's treasurer proposes paying the facilitators in cash without receipts to keep things simple.

c4.title: After-school reading club in Spanish Town
c4.text: A church and a primary school run an after-school reading club in Spanish Town for children aged 8 to 12, with ten adult volunteers. The coordinator is Mrs Pearl Grant. Several volunteers are young people from the congregation. Sessions take place in the school hall.

c5.title: Recycling education in Mandeville
c5.text: A six-month recycling education project in a Mandeville community ran eight weekly sessions for 150 registered adults. The project cost J$420,000 in total. A short quiz was given before and after the sessions.

questions.q: Dian wants to plan the project on firm evidence of where the problem is and why it happens. Which combination gives the fullest picture?
o: Health department case records, a household yard check and focus groups
The health department's case records only, because they are official, free and cover the whole parish
A household survey of the twenty homes that are easiest for her to reach on foot
Her own view, from living near the district for many years
questions.why: Records show the size of the problem, the yard check counts what people do, and focus groups explain why. Using several methods together gives the fullest and most reliable picture.

questions.q: What was the baseline percentage of homes with breeding sites, and why does Dian need it?
o: 45%, because the funder always asks the project to report its largest number
45%, since later results are judged against the starting point
30%, because it is the figure from the repeat check at the end of the project
20%, because it is the target figure that the final results are compared to
questions.why: 54 of 120 homes is 45%. The baseline is the starting measurement; without it you cannot show that anything has changed.

questions.q: The repeat check found 30 homes with breeding sites out of 120. What did the project achieve, and what should Dian report?
o: A fall of 24 homes, so the target was met and the report can simply say so
A fall from 45% to 25%, which is a 20% fall, so the target was fully met
45% to 25%, a fall of 20 percentage points, short of target
A fall from 54 to 30 homes, which should be presented to the funder as a complete success
questions.why: 30 of 120 is 25%. 45 - 25 = 20 percentage points. The target was below 20%, so it was missed. Report this honestly, with likely reasons, rather than claiming success.

questions.q: Which of these is a SMART objective for the next phase of Dian's project?
o: Reduce the number of mosquitoes across the whole parish as far as is possible in the time
Hold several more meetings with residents about mosquito control as soon as we can
Make sure that all residents are fully educated about dengue and its causes
By 30 June, 90 of the 120 homes checked will have no breeding sites
questions.why: It is specific (homes with no breeding sites), measurable (90 of 120), achievable and relevant to the need, and time-bound (30 June). The others have no number or deadline.

questions.q: The educator is preparing materials for the elders. Which choice is best?
o: A four-page leaflet of nutrition facts, printed in small type to save paper
A slide show with charts of imported foods, each with a long written caption
A demonstration with local foods and a picture plate, explained aloud
A written quiz at the end of each session to record everyone's scores
questions.why: Pictures, real examples and spoken explanation suit people with limited reading. Materials should use local foods and be tested with a few people from the group first.

questions.q: How should the educator best make sure the elders know about the sessions?
o: Post details on social media and rely on shares from the elders' younger relatives
Church announcements, health aides, word of mouth and radio
Send a text message with a link to an online registration website
Put one poster on the notice board at the municipal corporation's office in town
questions.why: Match the channel to the audience. Few of these elders use smartphones, so trusted local people and places reach them best. A single poster far from the community will miss most of them.

questions.q: At the first session an elder says, 'I have lived with sugar for twenty years; what can you teach me?' What is the best response?
o: Explain that his experience is out of date and he should follow the slides
Ask him to wait until the end so the lesson can stay on schedule
Offer to speak to him alone later so the group is not disturbed
Thank him, invite the group to share what works for them, and build on it
questions.why: Adults bring experience and learn best when it is used. Inviting people to share it respects them and gives the educator a chance to correct myths gently with accurate information.

questions.q: Participants say they can only reach town on Tuesdays, when the bus runs. What is the best change?
o: Fit the sessions to the Tuesday bus, or arrange transport
Keep the weekday afternoon slot and accept the lower turnout that results
Move the sessions to the next town, where there are more buses running daily
Ask participants to hire taxis at their own cost to attend
questions.why: Remove the barrier rather than blame participants. Fit the schedule to the bus, or provide transport (budgeted in the project). Always ask the target group what works.

questions.q: What is the total refreshment cost for the programme?
questions.why: J$250 x 50 people = J$12,500 per session; x 5 sessions = J$62,500. Work the sum a second way: 250 x 250 (people-sessions) = 62,500.

questions.q: What is the total planned cost, and how much of the J$400,000 grant is left unallocated?
o: J$354,500 total, with J$54,500 left
J$392,000 total, with J$8,000 left
J$354,500 total, with J$45,500 left
J$294,500 total, with J$105,500 left

questions.q: If all 50 young people complete the programme and the planned costs are spent exactly, what is the cost per participant?
questions.why: J$354,500 / 50 = J$7,090. Check: 7,090 x 50 = 354,500. Cost per participant is total cost divided by the number of participants, and should say whether it counts those who registered or finished.

questions.q: What should the coordinator say about paying the facilitators in cash without receipts?
o: Decline; every payment needs a signed receipt for the funder
Allow it, as long as the amounts match the agreed budget lines exactly
Allow it, but only for amounts under J$20,000, as those are small payments
Allow it, and write the financial report to the funder from the treasurer's memory
questions.why: Funders and auditors need evidence of spending. Cash payments without records cannot be checked and put the group, the coordinator and the funding at risk.

questions.q: A young volunteer offers to drive one of the children home alone because her mother is late. What should the coordinator do?
o: Allow it, as the volunteer has been vetted and attends the same church as the family
Allow it, but ask the volunteer to send a text message as soon as they arrive
Decline; the child waits with two adults until a parent or agreed adult comes
Allow it, because leaving the child waiting for a late parent would be worse for her
questions.why: Safeguarding rules say no volunteer is alone with a child out of sight, and children are released only to the parent or an agreed adult. Vetting does not remove that rule.

questions.q: A volunteer posts photos of the children at the club on his personal social media. What has gone wrong?
o: Nothing, because the club is an open public event in a school hall
No consent was obtained, and the code of conduct was broken
He should have blurred the faces of only the younger children
He should have asked the school, not the parents, for permission
questions.why: Photographs of children need the consent of a parent or guardian and must follow the project's rules. An open event does not give permission to publish.

questions.q: A child tells a volunteer, 'There's often no food at home on weekends.' What should the volunteer do?
o: Ask the child detailed questions until the volunteer is sure of all the facts
Visit the child's home that weekend to speak to the parents about it
Promise to keep it secret so that the child will keep on trusting her
Listen kindly, promise no secrecy, and tell the safeguarding lead that day
questions.why: The volunteer's role is to listen, record and report to the named lead, who follows the referral procedure. Volunteers should not investigate, confront family or promise secrecy.

questions.q: When should the police record check and references for each volunteer be completed?
o: Before the volunteer has any contact with children
After the first month, once the volunteer has shown they are reliable
Only for volunteers who are not members of the congregation
At the end of the term, when the funder asks for records
questions.why: Vetting is a safeguarding step that comes before contact. Waiting for a month, or checking only some volunteers, leaves children at risk.

questions.q: What percentage of the 150 registered adults is represented by 105 who attended at least six of the eight sessions?
The quiz average was 38% before and 71% after. Which statement is correct?
o: The average rose by 33%
The average rose by 87%
The average rose by 33 percentage points
The average rose by 109 percentage points
questions.why: 71 - 38 = 33 percentage points. Do not call it 33% because percentages are of different bases, and 87% would be the relative increase (33 / 38 x 100 = 86.8%), not the difference between scores.

questions.q: The 105 who completed the programme are used to work out the cost per completer. What is it?
questions.why: J$420,000 / 105 = J$4,000. Check: 105 x 4,000 = 420,000. Always say which count you use; per registered participant it would be J$2,800.

questions.q: Attendance fell sharply in the last two sessions, and the project missed its target of 90% completion. What should the final report to the funder do?
o: State the result, give likely reasons, and set out lessons learned
Leave out the last two sessions so that the attendance figures look much better
Focus on the photographs of the best-attended sessions and the happy faces
Blame the residents and the weather for the low turnout in those weeks
questions.why: Reports must be honest. A funder values results against aims, spending and lessons learned. Hiding or excusing a missed target damages trust and wastes the chance to improve the next project.
